brief.outcome: Move the Rails app's 380 GB, roughly 140-table MySQL 5.7 database to managed AWS RDS Postgres within three months with no data loss, and with customer-visible downtime at cutover of no more than 5 minutes (the point where a customer notice is needed), aiming for none.

ambition.goal_beyond: The app runs on managed Postgres with confidence, the old MySQL server can be switched off safely, and the team is not left with a migration that only looks finished.
rungs: Copy the data to RDS Postgres and switch the app over
Prove parity before the switch (data, behaviour and speed), rehearse the cutover and the way back, then cut over inside the downtime limit
Keep it true without being asked: keep a way back for a set period, run a standing reconciliation after cutover, and decommission the old server only when it keeps passing
ambition.judge: AWS DMS data validation and an independent row count and checksum comparison of source and target, the app's own test suite run against Postgres, and load balancer or app logs for the real downtime, none of them our own say-so

brief.deliverable: The app running on RDS Postgres in production, with a converted schema, the used stored procedures rewritten, a rehearsed and timed cutover runbook with a rollback, a parity readout, and a decommission proposal for the old server.
done: Source database inventoried and checked as migratable, with the blockers listed

Engineering manager chose the approach, cutover window and customer-notice rule

A full rehearsal on a copy done, with measured cutover time and a tested rollback
Production cutover done with approval at each step, within 5 minutes of customer-visible downtime
Row counts and checksums match on every table after cutover, with no data lost
Decommission and learning rules proposed for the engineering manager to accept or reject

research.approach: Practitioners separate a heterogeneous database move into three jobs that run in parallel: converting the schema and code (types, collations, stored procedures, SQL dialect), moving the data with a full load plus continuous change capture so the source stays live, and proving parity. The cutover is then a short, rehearsed event: let replication catch up, pause writes, check that nothing is pending, reset sequences, switch the app and keep a way back. They start from the raw source catalogue and logs, not a description of the schema, and they treat each unsupported feature in the tool's own limits list (primary keys, binlog format, cascade events, zero dates, 4 GB transactions) as a thing to test before choosing the approach. Stored procedures are migrated only if usage evidence shows they are still called.

sources.title: Using a MySQL-compatible database as a source for AWS DMS (AWS DMS User Guide)
sources.note: CDC needs binary logging on in ROW format with full row image, log retention long enough, replication privileges; limits: ON DELETE CASCADE events not propagated, AUTO_INCREMENT not migrated, binlog transactions over 4 GB, zero dates may land as null, TIMESTAMP converted to UTC. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Using a PostgreSQL database as a target for AWS DMS (AWS DMS User Guide)
sources.note: Load tables one at a time with foreign keys relaxed (session_replication_role = replica); update sequence values after replication stops because sequences are not migrated; type mapping table. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: AWS DMS data validation (AWS DMS User Guide)
sources.note: Compares each source row with its target row and reports mismatches in a control table; needs a primary key or unique index; stops after 10,000 failed records; adds load on both databases; views not validated. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

steps.name: Inventory the source from its own catalogue: tables, types, keys, collations, routines, triggers, sizes
steps.why: Every later choice rests on what is really in the database, not on a description of it.

steps.name: Scan the app for MySQL-specific SQL and for callers of stored procedures
steps.why: The dialect and the procedures are where the app breaks on Postgres; callers show which procedures are used.

steps.name: Check the source can be migrated and record a parity baseline
steps.why: Missing primary keys, binlog settings, zero dates and invalid values stop replication or validation; baselines make later checks meaningful.

steps.name: Test the migration risks one by one
steps.why: Types, collations, cascades, big transactions and timezones each need a different handling.

steps.name: Choose full load plus continuous replication, or another approach, with the cutover window
steps.why: The downtime limit and the 380 GB size decide the approach.

steps.name: Convert the schema, rewrite the procedures still used, change the app
steps.why: Converted objects and code must be tested on Postgres before data moves.

steps.name: Rehearse on a copy: load, replicate, validate, time the cutover and the rollback
steps.why: Rehearsal gives the real cutover time and exposes failures where they are cheap.

steps.name: Cut over: catch up, pause writes, verify, reset sequences, switch, keep the way back
steps.why: The sequence is short and ordered; sequences and cascades are the usual misses.

steps.name: Prove parity after cutover and watch the app
steps.why: Validation, checksums and app metrics show no data was lost and nothing slowed.

steps.name: Retire the old server only after a clean period
steps.why: Keeps a way back until parity keeps passing.

pitfalls.text: Starting replication before checking binary logging: enabling log-bin on the source needs a restart, which would itself cause downtime.
Forgetting to reset sequences after replication stops, so the first insert on Postgres collides with existing ids.
Relying on cascading deletes that replication does not carry, leaving orphan rows on the target.
Tables without a primary key are not validated, so a clean validation report can hide them.
Converting every stored procedure instead of checking which are used.
Zero dates, unsigned numbers and case-insensitive comparisons that load without error and behave differently.
Retiring the old server before a clean period, with no way back.

stages.name: Pin down the move
stages.goal: Turn the owner's words into a measured goal, limits and the access we have. Writes BRIEF.md.

stages.name: Inventory the MySQL database
stages.goal: Collect the catalogue, sizes, server settings and stored procedure usage into one folder, from the server's own tables.

checks.name: The number of tables is within 5 of the reported 140 and the total data size is within 10% of the reported 380 GB, or the difference is explained
Every table has columns, keys, collation and a row count; every routine has its definition
Procedure usage covers at least 30 days or is marked UNKNOWN for each procedure

stages.name: Scan the Rails app
stages.goal: Find MySQL-specific SQL, every caller of each stored procedure, other readers of the database, and how the schema is defined.

checks.name: Each MySQL-specific construct found lists file, line and the Postgres equivalent
Every stored procedure shows its callers or NONE FOUND
Scheduled jobs, reports and other apps that touch the database are listed or marked unknown

stages.name: Check the source can be migrated
stages.goal: Check primary keys, binary logging, zero dates, invalid values, case-only duplicates and foreign key orphans, and record row counts and checksums as the parity baseline.

checks.name: Tables without a primary key or unique index are listed (they cannot be validated)
log_bin, binlog_format = ROW, binlog_row_image = FULL and retention are recorded, with the restart risk if any is wrong
Counts of zero dates, out-of-range numbers, invalid UTF-8 and case-only duplicates under unique indexes are recorded per table
Row counts and checksums exist for every table, taken at a recorded time
Ends with READY, READY WITH FIXES or BLOCKED and the list that decides it

stages.name: Find what will break
stages.goal: Test the migration risk hypotheses against the inventory, code scan and readiness check, and decide for each stored procedure: port, drop with evidence, or unknown.

checks.name: Every hypothesis is SUPPORTED, REFUTED or UNKNOWN with the query result or file reference behind it
Every stored procedure is marked PORT, DROP or UNKNOWN with the usage evidence; DROP needs zero calls over the window and no code caller
Every column with a MySQL-specific type has a chosen Postgres type and a note on range or behaviour change
Each main finding names a competing explanation or a way it could be wrong

stages.name: Rank the approaches
stages.goal: Rank the ways to move: continuous replication with a short write pause, a tool-based migration with a longer pause, or a dual-write approach, each with downtime, risk, effort and cost.

checks.name: Every card states expected customer-visible downtime against the 5-minute limit and what it assumes
Every card cites the readiness and risk findings it rests on
Every card says how to go back to MySQL and until when

stages.name: Engineering manager chooses
stages.goal: The engineering manager picks the approach, the cutover window, what happens to each stored procedure marked DROP or UNKNOWN, and whether a customer notice is planned as a fallback.

checks.name: Chosen and passed-over approaches are recorded with the reason where the top card was passed over
Every UNKNOWN or DROP procedure has a recorded decision

stages.name: Prepare the conversion
stages.goal: Write the Postgres schema, rewrite the stored procedures chosen to be ported, patch the Rails app, write the replication task settings and the validation queries, and test the app on Postgres.

checks.name: The app's own test suite passes on Postgres, with the count of passing and failing tests shown, or failures are listed with causes
Each ported procedure has a test comparing its output on MySQL and Postgres for the same inputs
Only chosen changes are included; each patch names the finding it carries out
A second reviewer finds no unresolved blocker in the patches

stages.name: Rehearse on a copy
stages.goal: Restore a recent backup to a rehearsal environment, run the full load and continuous replication to a rehearsal RDS Postgres, validate, run the app tests and a read-traffic comparison, time the cutover steps, and drill the way back.

checks.name: Each AWS resource created for the rehearsal was approved first, with its cost estimate
Validation reports zero failed records and the independent row counts and checksums match for every table, or each exception is explained
Replication lag at peak load is recorded and returns to under 5 seconds
Each cutover step is timed and the total pause is under 5 minutes, or the plan changes
The way back to MySQL was drilled once and its time recorded

stages.name: Cut over production
stages.goal: With the engineering manager approving each step: confirm the rehearsal passed, let replication catch up, pause writes, verify, reset sequences, switch the app to Postgres, run smoke tests and keep MySQL read-only as the way back.

checks.name: Each production step has the engineering manager's approval recorded before it ran
Replication shows zero lag and zero pending validation before writes are paused
Every sequence is set above the maximum id of its table before the app writes
Write-pause start and end are logged from load balancer or app logs and total 5 minutes or less
MySQL is kept read-only and the rollback steps are ready until the manager retires them

stages.name: Prove parity and watch the app
stages.goal: Compare row counts and checksums on every table against the pre-cutover baseline, read validation results and app error rate and speed for 14 days, and measure the real downtime from the logs.

checks.name: Every table's count and checksum match the baseline plus the writes since, or the exception is listed
Customer-visible downtime is measured from logs, not estimated, and compared with 5 minutes
Error rate and request speed for 14 days are compared with the week before cutover on the same definitions
Any miss is reported with the numbers

stages.name: Keep what we learned
stages.goal: Propose when to retire the old MySQL server and what standing reconciliation to keep, and record the lessons for the next migration.

checks.name: The decommission proposal names the clean period and the checks that must pass first, and nothing is switched off without the engineering manager's yes
Each lesson says whether it holds for this app, this business or the playbook

hypotheses.statement: MySQL-specific column types need explicit handling.
hypotheses.test: Group information_schema columns by type: unsigned integers, tinyint(1), enum, set, year, json, zero-default dates.
hypotheses.confirm_if: One or more columns use types with no direct Postgres equivalent, or unsigned bigint values that exceed the signed range.
hypotheses.refute_if: All columns map directly with no range change.

hypotheses.statement: Zero dates or invalid values exist and will fail or change on load.
hypotheses.test: Count rows with 0000-00-00 dates and out-of-range or invalid UTF-8 values per table.
hypotheses.refute_if: Counts are zero on every table.

hypotheses.statement: Case-insensitive collation hides duplicates and lookups that break on Postgres.
hypotheses.test: Find groups of values equal under the MySQL collation but different in case or accents in columns with unique indexes; search code for equality lookups on emails and names.
hypotheses.confirm_if: One or more such duplicate groups or case-dependent lookups exist.

hypotheses.statement: Some tables have no primary key or unique index.
hypotheses.test: Tables without a primary key in information_schema.
hypotheses.confirm_if: One or more tables lack one.

hypotheses.statement: Many stored procedures are no longer used.
hypotheses.test: 30-day call counts from performance_schema plus code callers.
hypotheses.confirm_if: 30% or more have zero calls and no code caller.
hypotheses.refute_if: Under 10% are unused, or the usage data cannot be read, which leaves them UNKNOWN.

hypotheses.statement: The app has MySQL-specific raw SQL.
hypotheses.test: Search for backticks, ON DUPLICATE KEY, IFNULL, GROUP BY on non-grouped columns, FIND_IN_SET, STR_TO_DATE and similar in code and jobs.
hypotheses.confirm_if: One or more occurrences outside ORM-generated SQL.

hypotheses.statement: Binary logging is not ready for continuous replication, and fixing it would need a restart.
hypotheses.test: log_bin, binlog_format, binlog_row_image and retention from SHOW VARIABLES.
hypotheses.confirm_if: log_bin is off, or format is not ROW, or retention is under 24 hours.

hypotheses.statement: Cascading deletes or updates will not replicate.
hypotheses.test: Foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE or ON UPDATE CASCADE.

hypotheses.statement: Write volume or transaction size will make replication fall behind or fail.
hypotheses.test: Peak write rate and largest binlog transaction from the server; lag at peak in the rehearsal.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Any transaction near 4 GB, or lag stays over 60 seconds at peak in rehearsal.
hypotheses.refute_if: Largest transaction is far under 4 GB and lag recovers to under 5 seconds.

hypotheses.statement: The full load will take longer than the binary log retention.
hypotheses.test: Measured full-load throughput in the rehearsal against retention.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Projected full load plus catch-up exceeds retention.
hypotheses.refute_if: It finishes within half the retention.

hypotheses.test: Compare TIMESTAMP and DATETIME samples and the server time zone on both sides.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Any sample differs by a time zone offset.

measurement.window: The cutover itself from logs, then 14 days of app error rate and speed against the 7 days before.
measurement.min_volume: Every table is counted and checksummed, not sampled; app metrics are read over full days.
measurement.stop_rule: Roll back to MySQL if parity fails on any table after cutover, or if the write pause runs past the 5-minute limit and the rollback is cheaper than continuing.
